questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=9y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=9x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t) \\ -2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(2) \\ y(2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-2)}\,x(2) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-2)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-2)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-2)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-2))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-2))\, \\ \,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-2))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by  {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by substitution from lines {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from $\text{L2},$ we have the identity

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L3}.$ Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Substituting ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$ into $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L5}.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{substituting }{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}\text{ into }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$, $\text{L2},$ $\text{L5},$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L1}$ we have ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At},$ and from $\text{L5}$ we know $c=x(0).$ Substituting ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ from $\text{L1}$ and $c=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$ into $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ (line $\text{L2}$), we obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0).
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and substitution from $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L5}.$
